# Empirical Evaluation {#sec-results}

The preceding chapters developed the theory of GPs and DGPs and derived the variational inference framework needed for scalable training. This section evaluates both model families empirically, comparing them against standard machine learning baselines across three datasets that span different data characteristics, task types, and domains.

The first experiment uses the **Kin8nm** robot kinematics dataset (@sec-kin8nm), a regression benchmark with known non-stationary, compositional structure where we expect DGPs to outperform single-layer GPs. This establishes whether the additional depth of DGPs translates into measurable gains when the data warrants it.

The second experiment applies the same model families to financial credit-risk classification (@sec-credit-risk): probability of default on the UCI credit card dataset (@sec-credit-card). This smooth, monotonic risk surface tests whether DGPs add value on real-world financial data, while also evaluating the GP family's native probability calibration, which is of direct regulatory importance under Basel IRB [@basel_committee_basel_2011]. The aim is to assess whether the additional flexibility of DGPs gives a meaningful performance on a real financial data task.

Across both experiments, the model set comprises three classical baselines (linear model, random forest, XGBoost) and three GP-family models (SVGP, DSVGP-2L, DSVGP-3L). Each experiment evaluates performance at multiple training-set sizes to characterise scaling behaviour.
